why.headline: Strong legs push you up for high catches and dives.

claims.text: In studies of adult keepers, the big moments were dives and jumps. Both start with a push from the legs.
In studies with adult players, keepers jumped higher than outfield players.
In a youth trial, older teen players who added squats jumped higher. Their short sprints got faster too.
Children trained on machines once or twice a week. After 8 weeks, leg strength was 14 to 25% higher.
Older teen players added a weighted squat once a week. After 20 weeks, jumps were 4.5 to 4.9% higher.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The big muscles at the front of your thighs
The muscles at the back of your thighs
Your calf muscles, at the back of your lower legs

note.text: Squat studies measured these muscles in adults; none measured them in teens.

claims.text: In adults, letting the knees cave in changed which leg muscles worked.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested box squats alone in goalkeepers. The youth trials used weights, not bodyweight.
